articles.title: DC's Most Militant Superteam Had a Surprisingly Complicated History, and It's Time to Revisit Them
articles.summary: Image Courtesy of DC Comics DC Comics gave readers the first superhero in Superman, but they did fall behind in a certain place – militarizing the superhero. Captain America was the first major hero who was a part of the military and Marvel would take this trope further and further as time went on to the point that nowadays, if […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google DC Comics gave readers the first superhero in Superman, but they did fall behind in a certain place – militarizing the superhero. Captain America was the first major hero who was a part of the military and Marvel would take this trope further and further as time went on to the point that nowadays, if you're Avenger, you're basically a member of SHIELD and are a friend of the military industrial complex. DC's heroes were often patriotic, but one thing they never were pawns of the government. DC's heroes basically formed their own governmental body, one that existed to help the people. However, military heroes can be popular, so the company would begin branching out in those directions.

One of the interesting things about DC military characters is that they're often played as antagonists. They're often against the heroes of the Justice League and their allies or have joined for the purpose of watching them for the government. There are only a few big name DC military heroes, with the most well-known team being the Suicide Squad, and they're only ostensibly heroes or even military. However, there is another team of heroes who worked for the military who aren't a bunch of monsters you have to implant bombs in to get them to do what they're told. This group was introduced during Grant Morrison and Howard Porter's landmark JLA run, the perfect military heroes for the DC Universe. While they've rarely gotten the attention they deserve, they are pretty cool and it's about time for them to shine.

Grant Morrison has often made comics personal . Creators always use parts of themselves in their work ('70s Marvel is an example of a bunch of guys sitting around an office and writing about the movies they were watching and '70s NYC culture), and Morrison has taken that to new levels as they don their various "fiction suits" and enter into the world of two-dimensions. Usually, Morrison's more personal works were their Vertigo books, but they also brought parts of themselves into their superhero work, because Morrison's life was drastically changed by comics when they were a child.

Morrison's parents were both war protestors, their father having been in the British military. Morrison grew up with their parents constantly talking about the nuclear bomb and how dangerous it was. This terrified young Grant, this knowledge that at any time, an argument between two countries could vaporize our entire culture. However, there was an idea that was stronger to the young Scot – Superman. To Morrison, Superman – and by extension superheroes – were ideas that could beat the bomb. They were us at our best and if we were more like them, the world would be a better place.

For a creator like Morrison, military superheroes are almost an oxymoron, so any of them they created were going to be very different from the ones we're used to. This is where the Ultramarine Corps came into being. Morrison's JLA is one of the most beloved Justice League runs ever , and they worked hard to modernize the concept. They decided to bring back the Shaggy Man, an old school DC villain that was a remote-controlled indestructible body, with the shady General Eiling taking over as the new controller. Eiling created the Ultramarine Corps to act as his team, taking four Marines and giving them a metahuman gene.

They battled the Justice League, but soon broke away from the United States government, promising the team that they were leaving that life behind them. The group disappeared, but would return in the most Grant Morrison way possible – by having them create their own metahuman country, Superbia, and recruiting members from around the world to create a truly international superteam (partly by taking members from the Global Guardians). This occurred during the fantastic DC One Million , and one can see that there was a chance that Morrison was going to build the team into something cool at some point.

However, this wouldn't be the case, as the scribe left DC because of The Matrix (it's a long story that involved the Wachowskis ripping off The Invisibles and Warner Brothers fighting Morrison on it). They would lay fallow until Morrison's return to DC in JLA Classified #1-3, when they were fed to the Nebula Man as part of the build-up to Morrison's Seven Soldiers of Victory . Superbia would hold out against Darkseid during Final Crisis , which would be their final appearance.

The Ultramarines are the most Grant Morrison government team ever. They were given the chance to become superhuman but once they saw that they were being used by the powerful, they broke away and created their own super-society. The Ultramarines are an interesting idea that is honestly pretty perfect for the new DC Multiverse.

Grant Morrison is a different kind of comic writer, so any military superteam they create is going to be different. Morrison has an idea of superheroes as the ultimate expression of the goodness of humanity, and the Ultramarines fit perfectly into that. Morrison was a millennial optimist and their '90s work often played into this idea of a massive change that would lead us into a better tomorrow. Superheroes were all bound up in this belief and the Ultramarines are yet another example of that.

Think of it like this – these soldiers became metahumans and decided to make the world a better place not long after. There are numerous Morrison stories I can think of off the top of my head where this idea is the ultimate expression of hope. The Ultramarines take the idea of the military superteam and show that is fundamentally unsound. There can be no such thing as a military superteam, because superteams fight for everyone. The Ultramarines prove this and it's about time we talked about them more.

Do you remember the Ultramarines? What do you think about Morrison's superhero millennial optimism? Sound off in the comment section below.

articles.title: Much Has Already Been Said About Taxi Driver...I'm Here To Say Why It Still Matters In 2026
articles.summary: "Here is a man who would not take it anymore."
articles.content:
I love ‘70s cinema . In fact, if you were to ask me what my favorite decade of film is, I'd easily say the ‘70s. It just had so much grit and personality.

I once opined that the 1980s was Scorsese's best decade. However, I definitely think Scorsese's best movie came from the 1970s, as that's Taxi Driver . What's so potent about the film is just how mysterious Travis Bickle is as a character. I'm not the first to ask this (that would be Tarantino), but WAS Bickle really in the military, or was it just something that he concocted for himself to find purpose in his life? Is he seen as a hero at the end, or is it just his last dying wish?

I don't think I've ever heard a score that has been more instrumental to the greatness of a film than Bernard Herrmann's work on Taxi Driver .

When talking about the best Breaking Bad characters, Walter White usually comes to the top of the list. That's because he's the actual villain of the story, and it's up to the viewer to come to that conclusion.

I love the Rocky movies , but come on now. There is no way that the original Rocky should have beaten a movie like Taxi Driver for Best Picture.

The project stems from Raras' own experience of sexual assault as a teenager. Years later, she went through pregnancy herself.

articles.content:
Two prehistoric humans, one from the Philippines and one from Indonesia, cross paths as laborers in Spain in " Luz and Flor ," the new feature project from Filipino filmmaker Glenn Barit ("Cleaners"). The project, also known as "Luzonensis and Floresiensis," is among the 2026 JAFF Future Project selections at JAFF Market .

With Spain's property market collapsing around them, the pair look for a place to belong and a way to get by, while the echoes of colonial rule go unresolved. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Anya Taylor-Joy ‘Went Mute’ on ‘Lord of the Rings: The Hunt for Gollum’ Set When Ian McKellen Showed Up: ‘That’s F---ing Gandalf’

The project was recently selected for the International Film Festival Rotterdam's CineMart 2027 and won the Talents Tokyo Award in 2025. It took part in the QCinema Project Market in Quezon City, Philippines, in 2025, and has been through the West Meets East Screenplay Lab 2026 in Dhaka, the Film Development Council of the Philippines' Isapelikula Script Lab in Manila and the AFANxPaS Young Filmmakers Bootcamp 2026, held in Manila, Bangkok and Paris.

"When I was young, I used to frequent the caves where the bones of the Homo luzonensis were discovered. It is known to be the earliest ancient human species in the Philippines," Barit says. "So I became curious about this caveman character and the history that he might carry and represent."

A 2023 trip to Jogja, as Yogyakarta is known, left Barit struck by how alike Filipinos and Indonesians are, and how different. "I feel like we are two nations blurred by modern ideas of nations and borders," he says. Homo luzonensis is also thought to be a close relative of Homo floresiensis, a species found on Indonesia's Flores Island.

Barit wanted to drop the two characters into present-day struggles, as migrants in countries that once ruled their own. "I'm curious about these intersections as well as their ironies. How these supposedly 'primitive' figures might have something to say about our modern world," he says. "It also just seems exciting to research about and a bit funny to shoot." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

He is aiming for a tone that is thoughtful but playful. "Maybe a way of interrogating serious and tough questions through something absurd and imaginative," Barit says.

The film is produced by Kristine De Leon of the Philippines and Tanveer Hossain of Bangladesh through their company Katalog. The feature grows out of Barit's short "Luzonensis Osteoporosis," which played festivals abroad.

"Glenn Barit has an extraordinary ability to tell stories that feel fresh, inventive, and distinctly his own, without ever chasing trends," De Leon says. "Tanveer Hossain and I were immediately drawn to the short film. We found it beautifully crafted, thoughtfully directed, and full of creative possibilities."

The pair worked together for several years before setting up Katalog. "As producers from the Philippines and Bangladesh, we believe in bringing filmmakers and creative voices from different countries together through meaningful co-productions," De Leon says. "'Luz and Flor' is a wonderful example of this vision."

The screenplay is in its second draft, with the next draft underway, and the team is preparing for more research, notably in Spain, along with further creative consultations. Financing is planned for next year. At JAFF Market, the producers hope to bring Indonesian talent on board – a co-producer, a writing partner and a performer – to give the story's Indonesian side authenticity. They are also courting funders, sales agents and festival programmers.

Barit, meanwhile, is preparing a short backed by the Film Development Council of the Philippines that he will shoot 50 times, each time with a different cast, and is in early development on a romance feature about pet custody.

articles.title: A Forgotten Ferris Bueller Sequel Premiered in the '90s, With Jennifer Aniston Replacing One Character
articles.summary: As iconic 1980 movies go, there really aren’t any more iconic than Ferris Bueller’s Day Off. The John Hughes film starred Matthew Broderick, Mia Sara, and Alan Ruck in the story of a high school slacker (Broderick’s Ferris Bueller) who skips school with his best friend and girlfriend and things get a little wild. The […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google As iconic 1980 movies go, there really aren’t any more iconic than Ferris Bueller’s Day Off . The John Hughes film starred Matthew Broderick, Mia Sara, and Alan Ruck in the story of a high school slacker (Broderick’s Ferris Bueller) who skips school with his best friend and girlfriend and things get a little wild. The fourth wall breaking elements and overall humor made it pretty much an instant classic. And, as is the case with instant classics, everyone looks for ways to capitalize. In the case of Ferris Bueller’s Day Off , that came in the form of a forgotten sequel that featured Jennifer Aniston well before she’d star in her own piece of iconic entertainment.

On August 23, 1990, NBC debuted Ferris Bueller , a sitcom based on the Hughes film. However, while the series is seen as a sequel, it actually wasn’t canon or even a continuation. Instead, the series positioned itself to be the “real life” situations that inspired the film. The almost meta concept was a little strange and it didn’t exactly work. The series lasted for just one short, 13-episode season.

In Ferris Bueller , Charlie Schlatter plays Ferris and we very quickly have it established that this “real” Ferris isn’t happy with the movie or Matthew Broderick. The first episode literally has Schlatter’s Ferris use a chainsaw to destroy a cardboard cutout of Broderick’s Ferris. Once that’s out of the way, the show pretends the movie never existed. We get a focus on the cool guy Ferris, his friend Cameron (Brandon Douglas), love interest Sloane (Ami Dolenz), and sister Jeannie (Jennifer Aniston pre-Friends) and their times in high school at Ocean Park High in California.

Now, I’m not going to say that a Ferris Bueller television sequel would have worked in any format. The movie is kind of specific and very much its own, deeply loved thing. But the television series really didn’t have a good start. The concept was awkward, the recasting of beloved characters that were already a big part of pop culture never really took, and it was also just really poorly timed. The series had to compete with another, similar concepted series, Fox’s Parker Lewis Can’t Lose that was actually pretty popular. The deck was stacked against Ferris Bueller and that was almost immediately apparent. Critics hated it — the show got pretty much all negative reviews and has a 9% on Rotten Tomatoes. It did so badly that an NBC executive at the time noted that it was in danger of cancellation even before the ratings for the fourth episode hit.

The issue, ultimately, with Ferris Bueller is that it didn’t really capture or preserve any of what made the movie great. The recasts didn’t win anyone over (Schlatter’s Ferris was nothing like Broderick’s and not in a good way) but the series also took the story from Chicago to California. And that really didn’t work. A big part of Ferris Bueller’s Day Off is its setting. The city of Chicago is, in many respects, a character all its own. It’s very much Hughes’ love letter to the city he grew up in. Many Hughes films are set in Chicago, including another iconic film, Home Alone . Stripping the story of everything that made Ferris Bueller’s Day Off what it was doomed the show.

Of course, things ended up working out for Aniston. Even with Ferris Bueller being a disappointment, she went on to pick up some roles in other series (such as Quantum Leap) and eventually starred in 1994’s Friends , a series that would turn out to be one of the most popular shows of all time.

Did you know about the Ferris Bueller television series? Let us know in the comments.

A veterinarian's abducted teenage daughter comes home alive but emptied of her vital organs in " Primal ," the debut feature from Indonesian filmmaker Rein Maychaelson.

The body horror-thriller is among the titles selected for the 2026 JAFF Future Project and is being presented to the industry for the first time at JAFF Market .

Mira, a single mother in her 40s, has given up hope of seeing Lara again when the girl reappears months after her kidnapping. Lara cannot speak or remember anything, and a long line of stitches covers the empty cavity in her chest. When a savagely killed body turns up near the village, locals blame a tiger. Mira learns her daughter is the killer, and that each new organ makes Lara a little more human. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Anya Taylor-Joy ‘Went Mute’ on ‘Lord of the Rings: The Hunt for Gollum’ Set When Ian McKellen Showed Up: ‘That’s F---ing Gandalf’

To keep her alive, Mira fits a zipper to Lara's chest so that organs can be swapped for fresh human ones. With every replacement Lara grows more human and Mira less recognizable to herself, while suspicious villagers start looking closer to home.

Formerly titled "The Burning Land," the project won the fellowship prize at the Singapore International Film Festival's Southeast Asian Film Lab in 2022. It went on to the Busan Asian Film School that year, the Purple Tree residency in 2023 and the Chanel x BIFF Asian Film Academy in 2026, and recently picked up the Abroad Award at the Singapore festival's 2026 pitching forum.

"'Primal' grew out of my experience of watching my mother battle cancer. During that time, I became fascinated and frightened by the idea of losing someone while they are still physically present," Maychaelson says. "What if you recognize their face, their voice, and their gestures, but can no longer recognize the person behind them?" blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

The filmmaker describes the film as being about the limits of love and the terrifying acts people can justify when they are unable to let go. "Growing older, I've found myself questioning whether humanity is something we genuinely possess or simply something we've been taught to believe in," he says. "The myth of the extinct Javan tiger becomes another reflection of this tension: the stories we create to make sense of fear, survival, and truths we would rather not confront."

"Primal" is produced by Edwin Nazir and Astrid Saerong of Indonesia's Angka Fortuna Sinema, Sam Chua Weishi of Singapore's Potocol and Lee Dongha of South Korea's RedPeter Films.

"Rein is a promising director with a distinct voice," says Nazir, the project's Indonesian delegate producer. "'Primal' is a film I believe deserves a global audience, which shaped my approach in assembling our partners."

Saerong first came across Maychaelson's work in college and worked with him on his shorts "The Rootless Bloom," which played Busan in 2022, and "Sammi, Who Can Detach His Body Parts," which played the Berlinale in 2025. "'Primal' is a continuation of our long-time collaboration as he continues to interrogate and tries to understand the human condition," she says.

For Chua, the film is fundamentally about love and about what it means to be human. "At a time when we must re-examine our humanity with the prevailing violence around us, I am excited by this opportunity to work with Rein and the producing team to bring this profoundly emotional, elevated genre film to an international audience," he says.

The film is in advanced development and financing. After extensive research, location scouting and casting of the lead roles are underway, and the team is aiming to shoot in late 2027 or early 2028 and finish by the end of 2028. In Yogyakarta, the producers want one more producing partner to attach an editor, sound designer and composer, plus partners for post-production and distribution.

Maychaelson admits his outlook may sound a little like Quentin Tarantino's. "I like the thought of making only a handful of films in my lifetime. Knowing that I may not make an infinite number of them makes me value each project a little more," he says.

X-Men and Spider-Man paved the way, building off the sleeper hit that was Blade , before films like The Incredibles and Spider-Man 2 took the genre to a new level. In 2008, The Dark Knight grossed $1 billion and received Best Picture consideration, while Iron Man started the Marvel Cinematic Universe. Since then, superhero movies haven't looked back and have reached new levels of success, with the 2010s being the peak of the genre. It seemed like everywhere you looked, you could find a great superhero project on the big screen.

There were the obvious hits from the Marvel Cinematic Universe, there were major releases by DC from The Dark Knight Rises to the DCEU, and there were totally original superhero films. That's not even to mention great legacy sequels and animated features, which are all worth checking out. It would be incredible to go back and watch some of the best superhero movies from the 2010s for the first time again. That experience is hard to beat, especially when it comes to the best Spider-Man film ever made, which is certainly high praise to heap on a movie.

In a lot of ways, it feels like Logan had no business being as good as it was. The third solo outing for Wolverine followed up a bad first entry and a good, yet underrated sequel. The track record wasn't strong, but this 2017 film proved to be the best installment in the trilogy and possibly the peak of X-Men on the big screen . Logan took Wolverine into a future where he's old and his powers are waning, making him more vulnerable than ever.

Watching Wolverine develop his relationship with his daughter Laura was engaging and highly emotional. It's hard to remember another father/daughter dynamic that worked this well in a superhero film. Logan also featured the best performance by Hugh Jackman as Wolverine, a character he has portrayed across more than two decades. When you add in the deaths of Professor X and Wolverine, without knowing that we'd see the actors play these characters again, it hits even harder as a film.

It's hard to express just how much of a cultural phenomenon Black Panther was when it premiered unless you were there to experience it. Building off the titular character's excellent debut in Captain America: Civil War , this 2018 movie put him front and center while giving us our first true look at Wakanda. Ryan Coogler and the MCU crafted a gorgeous world that we'd all love to spend hours, if not days, in. The first time that we enter Wakanda is a magical movie moment that can't be replicated.

There's also the experience of getting to see Killmonger get revealed as T'Challa's cousin, which leads to their incredible encounter. It's the kind of thing that simply can't be recreated to the same effect. Just getting to be part of something that left such a lasting impact on the world's culture is awesome and, unfortunately, the fact that it ended up being Chadwick Boseman's only starring role as the character adds to what makes it so special.

DC released a lot of major movies during the 2010s, but many of them struggled or disappointed, like Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice and Justice League . A good place to look to find one of DC's best and most memorable projects is on the animated side of things with The LEGO Batman Movie . Released in 2017, a few years after the character stole the show in The LEGO Movie , this film manages to pay homage to the history of Batman and feature the kind of humor that LEGO movies are known for, which is a tough balancing act.

The animation style is pretty, but the real key to what makes The LEGO Batman Movie something worth experiencing again for the first time is the jokes. There are some legitimately hilarious moments here, from the explanation of Robin's shorts to the callbacks to old Batman movies to Batman saying that Bruce Wayne lives in Batman's attic; these are the kind of jokes that we'd love to hear for the first time.

2018 was a banner year for superhero movies as, just a few months after Black Panther , the MCU returned with Avengers: Infinity War . At the time, it was the biggest superhero film ever made, bringing the original Avengers together with Spider-Man, Captain Marvel, the Guardians of the Galaxy, Doctor Strange, and more. You simply can't beat the feeling of seeing all these characters share the screen, whether they were teaming up, bantering, or fighting with each other.

Of course, the film itself is a non-stop thrill ride filled with action that's so fun on rewatches. Yet, you can't match what it felt like in the movie theater to see Thanos come out on top. Watching our favorite Avengers turn to dust while you could hear a pin drop in the theater was something we can never match again. The scene still hits all these years later, but it will never be the same as that fateful first time.

When it comes to the best Spider-Man movie , there are several in the argument. Spider-Man 2 is a longtime favorite for many, while Spider-Man: No Way Home brought everything together expertly, and now Spider-Man: Brand New Day set box office records. However, the greatest Spider-Man film in history is 2018's Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse . The gorgeously crafted movie won Best Animated Feature at the Academy Awards for a reason.

While it's hard to top seeing Tom Holland, Tobey Maguire, and Andrew Garfield sharing a screen, Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse brought even more Spider-People together. We got our first look at Spider-Gwen on the big screen, while Spider-Noir, Spider-Ham, and others were well handled. Miles Morales is perfect, giving so many people a hero they can see themselves in. From the incredible soundtrack to the jaw-dropping visuals, this is a perfect movie, and the "What's Up Danger?" scene is legitimately the greatest ever.

What are your favorite superhero movie experiences from the 2010s? Let us know in the comments!

Channel 4 has been forced to defend its Huw Edwards doc three days before it premieres, with the network's news chief saying the film has "clear public interest."

Channel 4 unveiled Huw Edwards - Guilty last week and it will air Tuesday night. It has already been met with a barrage of criticism including from the upper echelons of UK government .

News chief Louisa Compton issued a rare and lengthy statement this morning, saying: "We understand that some people will profoundly disagree with our decision to make this film. But discomfort is not, in itself, a reason for journalism not to ask difficult questions. We believe those questions are in the public interest." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article1-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid","mid-articleX","mid-article","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[2,2],[300,250],[620,350],[300,251],[501,282],[3,3],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories News BBC Being Investigated Over Antisemitism By Government Adviser News Huw Edwards To Speak On TV For First Time About Criminal Actions & Fall From Grace In Channel 4 Doc

The statement came after the Prime Minister's spokesperson said the country has "no interest in hearing what [Edwards] has to say," while paying tribute to the "victims of child sexual abuse and exploitation." Compton joined with government in saying that behind Edwards' offences are "real children and real victims - including those as young as seven - who have been abused."

But she stressed that the disgraced ex- BBC News anchor "is not being allowed to tell his story unchallenged or on his own terms," and was not paid or given editorial control.

"Journalism isn’t about only putting people on television whose actions or opinions we approve of," she added. "Sometimes its purpose is precisely the opposite: to look directly at people who have done terrible things, confront them with difficult questions, test their explanations and allow audiences to judge what they say for themselves."

Compton, who was recently promoted to Director of News, Digital and Audience Trust, said the doc "raises wider and uncomfortable questions about power, trust and accountability, and about how our criminal justice system responds to people convicted of offences involving indecent images of children."

Airing on Tuesday night, the doc will be the first time Edwards has spoken publicly on TV about his conviction and fall from grace. He has addressed his actions on his Substack but this will be the first time he speaks about them with an interviewer. A short trailer sees Edwards say “I’d lost the plot” after being questioned over why he did what he did. The interviewer can then be heard saying exasperatedly, "Oh, come on.” blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dl-mid-article-inject2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article2","mid-articleX","mid-article","mid","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Allegations of grooming and paying younger people for sexually explicit images were published about Edwards in 2023 by The Sun and the following year he pled guilty to making indecent images of children. He has since mostly retreated from public life, returning to where he grew up in Wales, which is where the doc takes place.

“It is reasonable to ask why Channel 4 has made this film, and why now. As a public service broadcaster, we have a responsibility to think very carefully about what we put on screen, balancing the public interest in asking difficult questions of powerful people against the potential impact on our audiences, and particularly on victims and survivors of abuse.

We did not take that decision lightly. Journalism isn’t about only putting people on television whose actions or opinions we approve of. Sometimes its purpose is precisely the opposite: to look directly at people who have done terrible things, confront them with difficult questions, test their explanations and allow audiences to judge what they say for themselves. The circumstances and gravity are of course very different, but journalists routinely interview and hold to account people who have committed dreadful acts, including murderers, terrorists and dictators. The principle is the same: interviewing someone is not an endorsement of them. It is an opportunity to challenge what they have done, interrogate their account and allow audiences to judge their answers for themselves.

That is what this film does. Huw Edwards is not being allowed to tell his story unchallenged or on his own terms. He is questioned throughout by an experienced director; he was not paid; he had no control over the content of the film; and there were no restrictions on the questions he could be asked.

Edwards was one of the most prominent and trusted broadcasters in Britain. He pleaded guilty to serious offences involving indecent images of children and has never publicly faced detailed questioning about his criminal behaviour or the complete collapse of his career and reputation. There is a clear public interest in confronting him with those questions rather than allowing them to remain unanswered.

We are also acutely conscious that behind offences involving indecent images are real children and real victims - including those as young as seven - who have been abused. Nothing about making this film diminishes the seriousness of that harm, nor does Edwards’ participation entitle him to sympathy, redemption or rehabilitation. His account is there to be tested, not accepted.

Channel 4’s remit is also to stimulate debate. This film raises wider and uncomfortable questions about power, trust and accountability, and about how our criminal justice system responds to people convicted of offences involving indecent images of children. Those questions extend far beyond one disgraced public figure and deserve serious scrutiny.

Channel 4 has a long and established record of investigating powerful figures and confronting serious wrongdoing. That same journalistic instinct applies here: holding people to account sometimes means investigating them from the outside, and sometimes it means gaining access, challenging them directly and testing the account they give of their actions.

We should be capable of examining difficult issues rather than looking away because we don’t like what we see. We understand that some people will profoundly disagree with our decision to make this film. But discomfort is not, in itself, a reason for journalism not to ask difficult questions. We believe those questions are in the public interest.”

articles.title: The Worst Avengers Movie Did Something That No Other MCU Film Ever Did & It Was Awesome
articles.summary: Calling Avengers: Age of Ultron the worst Avengers film might sound harsh, but it's really just due to the high quality of the franchise. 2012's The Avengers remains a remarkable achievement that changed the face of the superhero genre, Avengers: Infinity War might be the pinnacle of the MCU in terms of storytelling and action, […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Calling Avengers: Age of Ultron the worst Avengers film might sound harsh, but it's really just due to the high quality of the franchise. 2012's The Avengers remains a remarkable achievement that changed the face of the superhero genre, Avengers: Infinity War might be the pinnacle of the MCU in terms of storytelling and action, and Avengers: Endgame masterfully culminated over a decade's worth of films satisfyingly. Avengers: Age of Ultron is a very good, highly entertaining movie that just so happens to have a lot of competition to be the best in its series of films.

The movie sits at a strong 75% on Rotten Tomatoes and did a lot of work in setting up the future of the MCU. The Infinity Stones were showcased, characters like Wanda and Vision were introduced, Steve's wielding of Mjolnir was teased, and more. However, despite all those things, Avengers: Age of Ultron is often viewed as the worst of the series, yet it does something that no other entry in the franchise has managed to pull off. Avengers: Doomsday is on the horizon and it looks like it also won't do what Avengers: Age of Ultron did so well, making that 2015 film all the more fun to look back on.

It sounds so simple, but Avengers: Age of Ultron gives us a look at the titular team actually working as a unit. Hearing that it's the only Avengers movie to truly do that sounds odd, since each film has them team up, but the way Avengers: Age of Ultron did it was different. Right from the opening scene, we're watching our favorite heroes work as a legitimate team. There is no in-fighting and they aren't only coming together because some world-ending threat like Ultron or Thanos is upon them.

The opening scene of Avengers: Age of Ultron features Captain America, Iron Man, Thor, Black Widow, Hulk, and Hawkeye fighting as a unit to retrieve Loki's scepter. It's a somewhat simple mission, yet the scene plays out like they've been working together often since the events of The Avengers . They're pulling out tandem moves like Thor slamming Mjolnir down on Cap's shield to take out a bunch of bad guys and they have a plan already set in motion for turning Hulk back into Bruce Banner through Natasha's "lullaby." The whole thing is a joy to watch.

The shot of every member flying into action feels like it was pulled straight out of a comic book and that's what longtime fans have always wanted to see. The scene also allows each hero a moment or two to shine while they work together. Natasha drives Clint around while both are shooting enemies, Cap is throwing his motorcycle at people, Iron Man is going after the scepter, Thor is just dominating foes, and Hulk is smashing. When you add in the fun banter between the team and the afterparty, this feels like the most harmonious iteration of the Avengers in the history of the MCU.

Again, it sounds odd to consider that other Avengers movies don't feature the team at their best, but it's true. In The Avengers , the characters didn't know each other, so they spent a lot of the movie at each other's throats. They do finally come together to save the day in the end, but they weren't a team in the same way that they are in Avengers: Age of Ultron . Unfortunately, the events of Captain America: Civil War prevented that team from ever truly being together again. Although Thor and Hulk were absent from that film, it shattered bonds for most other members.

One of the main reasons that Thanos was able to defeat the heroes in Avengers: Infinity War was because of how scattered they were. We see Cap, Nat, and Bruce working together, but Clint is nowhere to be found, Thor only joins his friends late in the game, and Tony is on another planet. The team never actually gets together. Avengers: Endgame sees them brought back together after Thanos' snap , but they are a much different team by that point.

Thor's confidence is shot, Clint has become more vengeful, and the rift between Cap and Iron Man was never truly settled. Also, they were all there with the stakes at their highest, while Avengers: Age of Ultron allowed them to just be a team on a regular mission. There's something simple and somewhat wholesome about that. Granted, there wasn't really room in the stories of Avengers: Infinity War and Avengers: Endgame to have missions like that, but that just makes the dynamic in Avengers: Age of Ultron more special.

The upcoming Avengers: Doomsday feels like more of the same, as the team is clearly not firing on all cylinders. Thor even says in the trailer that he doesn't know many of them and we've already seen them fighting amongst themselves, whether it's Shang-Chi against Gambit or Cyclops against Sam Wilson. The original team is also no longer around after the deaths of Tony and Nat, meaning we'll never see what Avengers: Age of Ultron gave us again.

What are your thoughts on the opening scene of Avengers: Age of Ultron and how the team has been handled in other movies? Let us know in the comments!

articles.title: 3 Cult '90s Fantasy Movies That Millennials Remember, But No One Else Cares About
articles.summary: In terms of entertainment, the 1990s were truly a golden era across multiple genres and formats, but it’s especially true for fantasy films. The decade gave audiences an absolute wealth of fascinating, creative, and unique stories that ranged everything from big budget blockbusters with incredible effects to smaller, quirkier movies that found their people on […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google In terms of entertainment, the 1990s were truly a golden era across multiple genres and formats, but it’s especially true for fantasy films. The decade gave audiences an absolute wealth of fascinating, creative, and unique stories that ranged everything from big budget blockbusters with incredible effects to smaller, quirkier movies that found their people on VHS rental shelves or on random Saturday afternoon cable broadcast. Some of those movies have gone on to become all time classics that appeal to not just the kids who enjoyed them back in the day, but to new generations as well, think films like Hocus Pocus and Hook .

But then there are the cult fantasy movies from the ‘90s that millennials remember and typically pretty fondly, that literally no one else cares about. These are the movies that were just weird enough or cheesy enough or that we saw on television enough that they’re carved into our memories. They’re the ultimate in nostalgia — and they deserve their time to shine. Here are three of them, including one that is surprisingly controversial because everyone remembers it wrong.

How 1991’s Drop Dead Fred isn’t more of an iconic movie that everyone knows and loves is honestly beyond me — Carrie Fisher is one of the movie’s stars, for goodness sake! The film, directed by Ate de Jong, also stars Phoebe Cates, Rick Mayall, Marsha Mason, and Tim Matheson and centers around a young woman (Cates) who is dealing with a lot of life setbacks that puts her in a pretty low place. It’s at this point that her childhood imaginary friend Drop Dead Fred (Mayall) returns to help. Chaos ensues.

The movie didn’t do well with critics and it wasn’t much of a box office hit, but it’s very charming. There is something just delightful about Elizabeth reuniting with her imaginary friend and finding her real self in the process. Not only does the movie beautifully reinforce the idea that you can grow up and heal and be stronger for it, but it’s fun. Oh, and bonus, a good chunk of the movie was filmed at Prince’s Paisley Park Studios.

This is a hill I will absolutely die on and it is that if you were a kid in the 1990s, you absolutely knew, loved, and still treasure The Pagemaster — and if you really loved The Pagemaster , you probably still love books and reading now. Released in 1994 starred Home Alone star Macaulay Culkin as Richard Tyler, a kid who is scared of literally everything. That includes storms so when a storm blows up, Richard seeks shelter in a library. Now, this ends up not being an ordinary library and he encounters the Pagemaster who takes him into an animated world where he has to battle through the literary classics to make it home.

Folks, The Pagemaster is so cool . Sure, the animation maybe isn’t great, but the idea of a scared kind learning to find his bravery by battling literary characters in an enchanted library rules. It gets even better when you realize who the voices of those literary characters and genres (who are also personified) are. Whoopi Goldberg is Fantasy, Frank Welker is Horror, and there’s even some serious Star Trek cred here with Leonard Nimoy as Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde and Sir Patrick Stewart as Adventure. This movie is so beloved by millennials that it could practically be a test to see if you are part of the generation — but even if you aren’t, do yourself a favor and check it out. It’s a real treat.

Okay, so everyone always thinks that Sinbad played a genie named Shazaam in a movie also named Shazaam but no such movie or role every existed. This is probably the most infamous version of the Mandela effect and there are indeed people who remain absolutely insistent that this movie exists. What is much, much more likely is that people are thinking of a ‘90s fantasy movie that every millennial knows and no one else cares about — other than to get the details wrong. That would be Kazaam . Released in 1996, Kazaam is a musical fantasy comedy that starred Shaquille O’Neal as Kazaam, a 5000-year-old genie who pops out of magic boombox to give a 12-year-old boy three wishes. As you can guess, there are some standard genie and wish granting hijinks.

What makes Kazaam memorable for millennials, however, might just be the emotional trauma it inflicted — which if we’re being honest isn’t that unusual for 1990s movies. Be nice to millennials, our entertainment is half the reason we need therapy. Near the end of Kazaam, Max (the kid getting the wishes) is killed when an adult shoves him down an elevator shaft. A heartbroken Kazaam wishes he could have granted Max’s final wish. That selflessness and heartfelt moment transforms Kazaam. He goes from genie to full on Djinn and his wish is granted. Max comes back to life. I told you: emotional damage. But worth it.

Writer-director Dhiwangkara Seta's feature debut is among the projects selected for the 2026 JAFF Future Project, a development platform at the JAFF Market. The […]
articles.content:
A teenage punk vocalist's arrest reunites him with his estranged father, a respected cleric, at a religious paramilitary boot camp in "Alpa (Absence)," a feature film in development at Lune Features.

Writer-director Dhiwangkara Seta's feature debut is among the projects selected for the 2026 JAFF Future Project, a development platform at the JAFF Market .

The story follows Banyu, a 17-year-old whose worldview is challenged when he encounters his father, Deri, at the camp. After years of resentment and longing for paternal affection, Banyu accepts Deri's offer to become his apprentice, gradually embracing the radical extremism his father espouses. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories 'Woman Unknown' Breakout Mathilde Arcel on Her Venice Award-Winning Performance and Life After Her Lido Triumph: 'Everything Is Open'

Things take a darker turn when Banyu witnesses Deri murder a young boy to protect his reputation as a respected commander of an Islamic organization.

"Growing up in the absence of a father, I was left without a blueprint for the man I was supposed to become. For years, I struggled with my own masculinity and sense of self," Seta tells Variety . "When I met my father again in my teenage years, he had become extremely religious and strict. I realized then that we could no longer speak the same emotional language."

In Southeast Asia, Seta adds, fatherhood is often tied to power and pride, with vulnerability hidden and affection rarely spoken aloud. "Through this film, I want to explore the cost of that silence – the pressure boys endure to embody a model of manhood that leaves no room for softness," he says. "I want to unpack how boys become men in the shadow of their fathers: by imitating them, resisting them, or trying to forgive them." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Seta previously made a short film of the same title, "Alpa," produced by QUN Films and Lune Features. Starring Elang El Gibran and Whani Darmawan, the film premiered at the 2025 Jogja-Netpac Asian Film Festival and later screened at the 2026 Clermont-Ferrand Short Film Market. It was also selected for the Asian Short Film Competition at the 31st Busan International Film Festival.

"Our film will use a father-and-son perspective to talk about the identity crisis that modern Indonesian society faces," says producer Eliza Cheisa. "Instead of focusing on the political aspect of the issue, we are more drawn to unveil the rawness of truth inside a man's journey and the family dynamics as two individual beings with their pain."

Cheisa also produced the short and previously worked with Seta on his debut short, "Samu the Terrible and His Sin," which won Best National Short Film at Bali's Minikino Film Week and screened at the Busan International Short Film Festival.

"Alpa (Absence)" is in development, with Seta currently writing the first draft of the screenplay. "Our main target right now is to receive development fund support in order for us to do our research on-site in Aceh and continue our script development until mid next year," Cheisa says.

JAFF Market, the industry arm of the Jogja-Netpac Asian Film Festival, runs Nov. 28–30 at the Jogja Expo Center in Yogyakarta. The festival's 21st edition runs Nov. 29–Dec. 6.

articles.title: 20 Years Ago, the X-Men Movies Lost Their Way for the First Time
articles.summary: Image Courtesy of 20th Century Fox Superman: The Movie is considered the grandfather of superhero cinema for a reason. Even though superheroes had been around for 40 years by then, a major Hollywood feature film starring one finally hit the screen. And even until the late 1990s, DC Comics was among the only major publishers getting its characters into movie theaters. […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Superman: The Movie is considered the grandfather of superhero cinema for a reason. Even though superheroes had been around for 40 years by then, a major Hollywood feature film starring one finally hit the screen. And even until the late 1990s, DC Comics was among the only major publishers getting its characters into movie theaters. Aside from Howard the Duck and Blade , Marvel had mostly kept its characters on television screens with both live-action and animated series. So in many ways, 2000’s X-Men created the template for the modern Marvel movies and eventually the MCU would follow.

Despite the creative liberties that first movie took with the source material , fans were willing to overlook the black leather outfits, absent character backstories, and reduced screen time for characters like Cyclops. Both X-Men and especially 2003’s X2: X-Men United treated the Marvel mutants with such reverence that fans largely accepted them with open arms. Nightcrawler’s opening assault on the White House, Wolverine’s berserker rage during the attack on Xavier’s school, and hints at Jean Grey’s latent Phoenix Force gave fans just a taste of the epic moments the MCU would ultimately deliver. But 20 years ago, fans’ goodwill toward Fox’s X-Men films ran out.

The first sign of trouble came when director Bryan Singer — who helmed the first two films — opted out of returning for the then-untitled X-Men 3 . Instead of staying with the franchise, Singer went off to Warner Bros. to make Superman Returns , taking composer John Ottman, writers Dan Harris and Michael Dougherty, and actor James Marsden with him. Enter Brett Ratner, director of the Rush Hour films and the Hannibal Lecter sequel Red Dragon . That change in hands then led to a new script by Simon Kinberg and Zak Penn, one that combined the Dark Phoenix Saga teased in X2 with the “Gifted” arc centered on the creation of a mutant cure.

Despite its grand scope, X-Men: The Last Stand somehow clocked in at just 104 minutes, the same length as the first film. And while it became a box office smash overall, fans and critics were not having it. Marsden’s Cyclops was killed off-screen early in the film, Juggernaut became a joke, and the rushed story failed to do justice to either Dark Phoenix or the mutant cure. Even though the movie delivered a Danger Room sequence (finally) and gave fans Kelsey Grammer’s beloved take on Beast, the film failed to live up to its predecessors. Instead, it became just another trilogy-ender that let audiences down, breaking the series’ streak of winning over fans.

Unfortunately for the franchise, X-Men: The Last Stand was only the beginning of a series of baffling creative choices. With its core trilogy over and done with, Fox intended to shift its focus to a series of origin stories focused on individual X-Men characters. So, despite being essentially the main character of the preceding trilogy, the first one produced was X-Men Origins: Wolverine . But bad visual effects, a weak script, and an embarrassing depiction of fan-favorite Deadpool sunk the movie among fans, proving once again that Fox just didn’t get it. The X-Men Origins concept was abandoned in favor of a reboot film, X-Men: First Class , which was ultimately retconned into a prequel to the original trilogy with X-Men: Days of Future Past .

After First Class , The Wolverine , and Days of Future Past — the latter of which marked Singer’s return to the franchise — it seemed like the series was back on track. The time-travel shenanigans in Days of Future Past not only prevented a dystopian future but erased both X-Men Origins: Wolverine and X-Men: The Last Stand from the timeline. But that goodwill was once again squandered with two unsatisfying sequels, X-Men: Apocalypse and Dark Phoenix , the latter of which again tried (and failed) to bring the beloved storyline to the screen. While Logan and the Deadpool films helped salvage what was left of the Fox X-Men universe, The New Mutants certainly ended things on a sour note. articles.title: Indonesian Cinema's Next Chapter Is Reaching the World 'Without Losing Our Cultural Identity,' Says JAFF Market Director Linda Gozali
articles.summary: Indonesia's film industry has momentum at home. JAFF Market director Linda Gozali wants to help it travel. Gozali runs the industry market attached to the Jogja-Netpac Asian Film Festival (JAFF), now in its third edition. The 2024 launch tested whether Indonesia needed a film market at all, and the industry's answer was an emphatic yes. […]
articles.content:
Indonesia's film industry has momentum at home. JAFF Market director Linda Gozali wants to help it travel.

Gozali runs the industry market attached to the Jogja-Netpac Asian Film Festival (JAFF), now in its third edition. The 2024 launch tested whether Indonesia needed a film market at all, and the industry's answer was an emphatic yes. The 2025 edition opened the door to regional and international partners. This year, the market is taking stock of how well the business holds up against economic turmoil and political instability around the world, while widening the scope for credible partnerships at home and abroad. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Oscar Predictions: Film Editing — ‘You Can See Everything’ Looks to Crash a Race of Past Winners and Become the Third Documentary Ever Nominated 'Hold Onto Me' Director Myrsini Aristidou Kicks Off Historic Oscar Campaign for Sundance Audience Award Winner: 'I Really Feel Like We're Underdogs'

"Our next chapter is learning how to reach international audiences without losing our cultural identity," Gozali tells Variety. "We aspire to become nationally indispensable, regionally relevant and internationally connected."

Local hits have yet to translate into comparable business abroad, which Gozali puts down to producers and filmmakers treating the home market as their first priority. "Indonesia has learned how to win its own audiences," she says, adding that plenty of untapped local viewers still need to be brought in.

Even so, Gozali says, a good share of Indonesian horror has sold across multiple territories, and independent films have been well received on the international festival circuit. She also notes that Indonesia is not alone in looking inward first, pointing to other populous countries such as China, India and Japan.

"Any growth should not be mistaken for maturity," she says. "JAFF Market's responsibility is to transform that growth into sustainability." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

That thinking draws on an industry report JAFF Market produced with Cinepoint. According to Gozali, it points to a basic mismatch between Indonesia's volume of content production and appetite for investment on one side, and its limited exhibition infrastructure on the other.

"Sustainable growth requires wider audience access, diversified distribution access, responsible production investment and stronger business intelligence," Gozali says. "Our collaboration with Cinepoint is intended to encourage evidence-based industry decisions."

The market can already point to results. Projects that have met collaborators for their next steps include "Pangku" and "My Mother" from JAFF Future Project (JFP), and "Tikam Samurai," "Bandits of Batavia," "World Without Sleep," "Timun Mas" and "Gloomy Sunday" from the JAFF IP Connection (JiPCon) strand. Joint ventures, memorandums of understanding and letters of intent have also emerged around "Khadam" and "Badut Gendong," along with an agreement between JAFF Market and the Jakarta government.

Gozali singles out "Slaughterground" as the clearest example of the market linking things up over time. Presented as an IP at JiPCon during the 2024 inaugural edition, it returns this year as a film in JAFF Future Project. "The IP met its destiny in JAFF Market," she says.

The deals, she argues, have created value beyond the event itself. But she sees the market's main achievement as bringing the whole of Indonesia's film industry under one roof for the first time.

JAFF Market shares the regional calendar with Busan's Asian Contents & Film Market (ACFM), Hong Kong FilMart and the Taiwan Creative Content Fest. "We are the new kids on the block so we want to work alongside the other established markets and learn and partner with them in areas that will strengthen our programs and also theirs," Gozali says.

Every market hopes to become a long-term international hub, she adds, but JAFF Market will take it one step at a time. Some ties are already in place. The market continues to collaborate with the Adelaide Film Festival, an institutional partnership Gozali says brings continuity, credibility and a route into established international networks. It also runs a reciprocal IP exchange with ACFM.

To bring in international sales agents, distributors, financiers and streamers, the market relies on curated programs, business dialogues and matchmaking designed to move attendees from general discovery toward focused meetings with decision-makers. "We recognize that international participation must be driven by business opportunities, not simply invitations," Gozali says. "The quality and relevance of international participation matter as much as the number of delegates or countries represented." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

"As a producer myself, I recognize that one of our industry's gaps (besides a shortage of stories or talent), is a shortage of sustained cross-border producer relationships," she says of the market's Producers Exchange strand, which aims to build trust, encourage knowledge sharing and help producers find compatible partners beyond one-off projects. "Connecting the right producers today can shape the regional production and distribution landscape of tomorrow."

For newcomers, JAFF Future Project, Film Labs and Talent Day offer a way into the Indonesian industry. Gozali says the insights gathered across the market's programs help first-time filmmakers find their way and have shaped how they handle business with international partners.

International co-productions open up additional financing, creative expertise, shared resources, distribution networks and new audiences. Indonesia, however, would benefit from clearer regulatory frameworks, production incentives and tax rebate mechanisms. "It is important to ensure that Indonesian filmmakers are ready to become equal creative and business partners," Gozali says.

JAFF Market is backed by Amar Bank, Indonesia's Ministry of Culture and Ministry of Creative Economy, Jakarta City and a roster of sponsors and partners. Gozali is grateful for that backing but says the platform needs long-term, sustained support in both funding and infrastructure to keep serving the industry.

"JAFF Market must remain commercially responsible without becoming commercially exclusive," she says. Diversified revenue streams, strategic partnerships and curated programs are meant to keep the market open to independent filmmakers and emerging production companies. "Supporting emerging talent is not simply a philanthropic endeavor; it is an investment in the industry's future creative and commercial potential," she adds.

As for the next five years, "Growth is not necessarily about becoming bigger," Gozali says. "It is about becoming more relevant, useful and consequential."

articles.title: Southeast Asian Cinema's Global Rise Needs Long-Term Backing to Last, Says JAFF Chief Ifa Isfansyah
articles.summary: The quality and international profile of Southeast Asian cinema have grown sharply, and Ifa Isfansyah, festival director of Indonesia's Jogja-Netpac Asian Film Festival (JAFF), wants countries to build on that by treating film as part of their cultural strategy. He singles out the Philippines for its consistency in developing talent and keeping a presence abroad. […]
articles.content:
The quality and international profile of Southeast Asian cinema have grown sharply, and Ifa Isfansyah , festival director of Indonesia's Jogja-Netpac Asian Film Festival (JAFF), wants countries to build on that by treating film as part of their cultural strategy.

He singles out the Philippines for its consistency in developing talent and keeping a presence abroad.

"I would say that, for now, it is still more of an anomaly than a fundamental structural shift," Isfansyah tells Variety . "However, international recognition is still largely driven by the strength of individual films and filmmakers, rather than by a broader, sustained strategy to strengthen cinema as part of a country's cultural infrastructure." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Is ‘I Play Rocky’ Original or Adapted? Stallone’s ‘Rocky’ Origin Story Faces a ‘Barbie’-Style Oscar Dilemma (EXCLUSIVE) Sweden’s Oscar Entry 'Adult Supervision' Closes Further Deals (EXCLUSIVE)

Isfansyah is also one of Indonesia's leading independent producers. He founded Forka Films, formerly Fourcolours Films, in 2001, and his producing credits include Kamila Andini's "Yuni" and "Before, Now & Then," as well as her latest, "Four Seasons in Java," which played Toronto's Centerpiece program and Busan this year.

"I believe countries need to recognize cinema as an important part of their cultural strategy, not merely as an industry or a source of national prestige," he says. "This requires long-term investment, institutional support, and a commitment to building sustainable connections with the international film community."

JAFF's 21st edition drew more than 1,000 submissions, from which the festival picked 254 films from 34 countries. The program runs under the theme "Influx," opening with Lawrence Fajardo's Filipino drama "Silenced Nights" and closing with Ueda Makoto's Japanese comedy-drama "You Are the Film." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Isfansyah says the current social, political and economic climate pushed the team to rethink what staging a festival should mean this year. "We did not want JAFF to become a celebration disconnected from the realities around us. This is not a moment for an excessively festive atmosphere or for pretending that everything is fine."

Fajardo's film, he says, speaks directly to present-day anxieties. Opening with it was meant to signal that "cinema must remain connected to the world we live in, and a festival should not be afraid to confront difficult realities."

The closer is pitched partly at younger viewers, as a reminder of where JAFF came from. "JAFF began with a love for films like this, films that may not necessarily be grand in scale or production, but possess sincerity, imagination, and a strong cinematic voice," Isfansyah says. "I think it is important to remember that a film does not have to be big to be powerful."

Among the submissions, he noticed filmmakers growing bolder, especially in shorts, with more of them playing with form and blurring fiction and nonfiction. "Short films are increasingly becoming spaces for creative risk-taking," he says, rather than mere stepping stones to features.

Many films were also more political, though not always in the sense of tackling institutions or specific events. "There is a growing urgency to tell stories that respond to the realities surrounding us."

The "Influx" theme also nods to change across Asian cinema, from a new generation pushing against established storytelling to shifts in how films get financed and reach audiences. "However, I think it is important to look beyond the idea of change as simply a matter of technological or industrial transformation. We should also ask where these currents are taking us, whose voices are shaping the direction of Asian cinema, and what kind of future we are building together," Isfansyah says.

On Indonesia's local box office boom, he sees no hard line between the country's commercial, arthouse, independent and genre directors. "Many filmmakers know one another, compete in a healthy way, exchange ideas, and often support each other's work," he says. Commercial hits, he adds, pull more people into cinemas, lift interest in local titles and draw investment, while challenging independent work keeps the industry diverse and credible. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Premieres matter, but they have never been JAFF's main yardstick. What counts is whether a film merits a slot and whether it has already had a fair shot at the festival's audience. "If we believe a film has not yet had the opportunity to reach JAFF's viewers, we will be interested in bringing it here, regardless of whether it has already premiered elsewhere."

As it enters its third decade, the festival wants to put back into the ecosystem that built it. This year it launched JAFF Kids, aimed at children and young audiences, and JAFF Awards, which honors individuals, institutions and initiatives in Indonesia and the wider region that have helped develop film culture. Earlier programs JAFF Community Forum and JAFF Market grew strong enough to become parallel events in their own right.

However large JAFF gets, Isfansyah says it has to keep resting on emerging talent, industry professionals and academics, and keep all of them talking to one another.

"For me, being community-driven does not mean remaining small. It means remembering that the festival exists because of the people who build it, participate in it, and give it meaning."

articles.title: France Knights 'Autobiography,' 'Tiger Stripes' Producer Yulia Evina Bhara at JAFF Market

Fabien Penone, France's ambassador to Indonesia, Timor-Leste and ASEAN, presented the insignia for France's culture minister. The ceremony […]
articles.content:
Indonesian producer Yulia Evina Bhara , whose credits include Venice title "Autobiography" and Cannes Critics' Week winner "Tiger Stripes," was named a Chevalier dans l'Ordre des Arts et des Lettres at a ceremony at JAFF Market in Yogyakarta.

Fabien Penone, France's ambassador to Indonesia, Timor-Leste and ASEAN, presented the insignia for France's culture minister. The ceremony doubled as the opening of the Indonesia-France Film Lab booth at the market, which runs Nov. 25–30. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Governors Awards 2026: Glenn Close, Ridley Scott and More Receive Honorary Oscars From The Academy (Live Updates) Marvel’s ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ Won’t Screen for BAFTA, Golden Globes and Other Early Awards Groups to Guard Its Spoilers (EXCLUSIVE)

France created the order in 1957, and its cinema honorees range from Agnès Varda, François Truffaut, Martin Scorsese and Isabelle Huppert to Indonesia's Garin Nugroho. Filmmaker Joko Anwar received it last year.

"When I read the names of the people who received this before me, I felt very small," Bhara said. "They are writers, painters, musicians, directors, and many of them are my heroes. So when the letter came, my first thought was, maybe this is a mistake. My second was, this is not only for me, and this is true. A film producer never works alone. A producer is like a person who builds a boat, but the boat only moves when people row together."

In his address, Penone traced Bhara's path from Way Kanan in Sumatra's Lampung province through seven years of producing historical theater, a craft she taught herself, before she turned to film in 2012 with a foundation that used art to revisit the past. She set up KawanKawan Media in Jakarta in 2016, with international co-production at the core of the business from day one. The company's name is Indonesian for "friends."

Its first feature, Yosep Anggi Noen's "Solo, Solitude," bowed at Locarno that year and later took the Golden Hanoman Award at the Jogja-Netpac Asian Film Festival . Makbul Mubarak's "Autobiography" premiered in Venice in 2022 and went on to become Indonesia's Oscar submission. "Tiger Stripes" won the Critics' Week Grand Prize in 2023, and Bhara co-produced "Renoir," which played in competition at Cannes in 2025. That same year she sat on the Critics' Week jury. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

This year she co-produced Next Step Studio Indonesia, which launched as the Critics' Week's new talent initiative and paired four young Indonesian filmmakers with four from across Southeast Asia. The result premiered at Cannes to a standing ovation. Bhara also heads international cooperation at the Indonesian Film Board (BPI), is active in producers' body Aprofi and has been one of the Film Lab's driving forces since its launch.

"Without question, you rank among the most respected producers in Indonesia," Penone said. "Your work has helped Indonesian cinema reach new audiences and gain new recognition."

Bhara, who said she grew up in a small village by a forest and that her family was very poor, recalled that one of the first films she ever watched was Nugroho's "Cinta dalam Sepotong Roti," and that nearly every film she has produced was a multi-country effort, with partners from Singapore, Malaysia, the Philippines, Japan, Taiwan, Germany, Poland, Qatar and France.

She told the room that independent cinema now faces three pressures, the first being big money and content, with young directors often told their stories are too small and too local. "I believe the opposite: the more local a story is, the more universal it can become," Bhara said. "Second, attention. Fifteen seconds, then we swipe. But cinema is the art of staying. The third, the machine. AI can make images, the voices in a second, but a machine cannot remember what it feels like to lose someone."

The Film Lab is run by the French Embassy and Institut Français d'Indonésie together with Indonesia's Ministry of Culture, BPI and Aprofi, backed by French film agency CNC and Paris film school La Fémis. Six Indonesian director-producer teams were picked this year, with Éric Collin, Vincent Wang, Thibault Amti and Sébastien Chesneau among the mentors. The lab continues for the next six months.

"A first edition is an experiment. The second one is a test. A third edition tells us that something has become a habit, an institutional relationship," said BPI chair Fauzan Zidni, whose organization joined the initiative for the first time this year. A producer who has chased international co-productions for 14 years, Zidni said he had gone to markets alone in search of partners, and pledged that BPI would keep supporting the projects after the lab ends. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Penone said most projects from earlier editions will head to Paris early next month for the Southeast Asia Film Forum's inaugural co-production meetings, staged with CNC backing and the Centre Pompidou as partner. BPI members and filmmaker Edwin will also attend.

"Chevalier means a knight. A knight promises to protect something," Bhara said. "So today, I promise I will keep protecting the fragile voices, the local films, the human films, and I promise I will never do it alone."

The Universe 6 Saiyans give us that alternate timeline in Dragon Ball Super , as they flourished as a peaceful nation that didn't make its living conquering other worlds. The story of the Saiyans in Universe 7 is one of tragedy, but also plenty of self sabotage. The Planet Sadala Saiyans match up much more with Goku, Vegeta and the other Saiyans living on Earth. They defend what they love and their intentions are pure.

Cabba, Caulifla and Kale proved a quality trio in protecting their world in the Tournament of Power. Although they aren't violent in nature like their sister universe Saiyans, when a fight comes their door, they answer the call. Universe 6 lasts a good chunk of the tournament, but it's not nearly as strong as Universe 7. An arc about Goku and Vegeta training Universe 6 Saiyans and getting into a conflict with a rival planet would give fans new Saiyans to follow and potentially a whole new series offshoot.

In comparison to the beginning of Goku and Vegeta's journeys as Saiyans, Cabba, Kale and Caulifla appear to be starting at a higher base level. The latent potential of the trio is higher than Goku, who achieved what he has through relentless work ethic. Those three gain a lot of their transformation power through getting enraged, instead of through standard work. This isn't a bad thing, as it shows what they're capable of with just a small push. However, it also shows there is a lot left to gain, especially with Kale who definitely drew comparisons to the original Broly with her Super Saiyan Berserk mode.

It takes quite a bit of pushing to get them into the fight, so maybe the new arc could be about their home world of Planet Sadala coming under threat. Vegeta takes Cabba under his wing and gets him ready for war, as they both feature deep pride in their Saiyan roots. While Caulifla and Kale work with Goku and Broly respectively to get the most out of their matching styles.

Caulifla might not match up with all the good traits of Goku, but her passion for fighting the strongest of the strong is just like him. Kale and Broly are meek fighters that turn into uncontrollable monsters at the peak of their powers. A hallmark trait of recent media put out in the Dragon Ball universe is that base forms carry a lot more power than they used to. These three carry that same trait and could give Goku and Vegeta a lot of potential to work with, and eventually good fighters to add to their team. Furthermore, a recent trend is bringing lower level Super Saiyan forms back into the mix, and all three haven't gone above Super Saiyan 2.

Universe 6's Saiyans may feature good-natured personalities in comparison to their battle-hardened brethren, but don't let that fool anyone. These Saiyans still share a fierce, protective love for their race with Universe 7 . A new series featuring the Universe 6 Saiyans can dive into that part of their DNA more. It's the protagonist race of the series, but it's not seen in its original element on an actual home world.

A trip to Sadala gives the fans a genuine look at that, essentially Planet Vegeta in the present. From low-level Bardocks to the high-level royals like King Vegeta, it'd open up a lot of possibilities for the Saiyans in Dragon Ball Super . Furthermore, the war that tore the other Saiyan planet apart would get a complete redo in this timeline. Cabba, Kale and Caulifla get to decide the fate of their planet from the very beginning. No servitude to an evil ruler, infighting amongst each other, and it would be just a great chance to keep the peace and defend the world from the traits that turned the original Saiyans into power hungry savages.

Goku and friends want to see them survive and thrive, but also know there is a constant threat from anywhere in the multiverse. Although the trio is a bit more diminutive than the Universe 7 Saiyans, their ability to transform and grow at a rapid rate shows how well they tapped into their Saiyan pride. Do you think Dragon Ball Super should do an arc on the newest Saiyans? Let us know in the comments.
